# The shape of the day

**Two goals, as always:** they leave knowing these tools do far more than they
thought, and believing they can do it themselves on Monday. Everything else is in
service of that.

**A spine and a menu.**

- **The morning spine is fixed, and all of it is mandatory.** Everyone gets
  running with git, has the agent do something tedious on a messy folder (with a
  save point and an undo), writes a profile, and has the agent take their own paper
  apart. The "get started" goal is met by lunch, whatever happens after.
- **The afternoon is a menu.** Referee panel, References, Leave a trail, Notes and
  structure. Referee panel and References work on the paper folder from the
  morning; Leave a trail brings its own practice folder. Any subset in any order
  makes sense.
- **There's no pressure to cover the menu.** The menu slide and the handout show
  the whole range. That *is* the range lesson, even for blocks we never open. Doing
  two modules well beats four in a hurry.

**Where things are.** One deck per module in `decks/`. Open **`decks/menu.html`**
first: every card opens a module's deck, and **Menu** in each deck's footer comes
back. Inside a deck, press **M** for the slide list and **Esc** for the overview.
`handout.html` has every prompt with a copy button, section-numbered to match the
slides.

| Deck | What | Minutes |
|---|---|---|
| `menu` | Title, the menu, "one folder", start the install | 10 |
| `power` | Capability talk: programming, maths benchmarks, a released model on open problems, Navier–Stokes, the 6 October results, "the biggest day in history?", Duminil-Copin; ends on a teaching slide (an animation written as code) | ~10 |
| `how` | What an LLM is (training: pre-training, feedback, RL; use: thinking), prompt engineering (RIP), what an agent is, usage limits | 6 |
| `setup` | Install, log in, git (required), which model and limits, first contact | 45 |
| `git` | Save points: what git is, where it comes from (timeline, two charts), for the agent, vs OneDrive, .gitignore, the cloud, five words, ask about the rest, GitHub and Pages. Four exercises | 30–35 |
| `access` | What it can touch: how far each tool reaches, what leaves the laptop, the dial, auto mode, what we tried, why lots of access, three ways to say no, training switches, personal data. Three exercises | 20–25 |
| `cleanup` | Do something tedious: the WISEflow export, with a git save point and an undo | 25 |
| `knows` | Context, who is asking, the Berger demo, does it matter in your field, how you work, your profile | 20 |
| `paper` | Take a paper apart; ends on the afternoon choice | 50 |
| `review` | Referee panel | ~40 |
| `refs` | Search (exercise), papers in the folder, DOI check, claim check | 40–60 |
| `trail` | Organise a folder, the rerun test, what the rerun found | ~50 |
| `notes` | Four questions, structure, notes, project file, skills | 20–30 |
| `own` | Open lab and close | 30+ |
| `agents` | If asked: the project file, one `AGENTS.md` for both tools, asking for changes | 10 |
| `github` | If asked: git vs GitHub, setup, co-authors, public or private | 10 |
| `mcp` | If asked: connectors (MCP), switching one on, one example each for email, calendar, Drive | 5 |
| `more` | Backup: security, benchmarks, Eco, Concord, prompting; the long capability talk | as needed |

# Before Friday

1. **Links: done.** All practice files are on GitHub `main` and tested. The
   handout's download prompts (sections 2, 6, 7) use the GitHub links; the decks
   point to the handout.
2. **TODO: go through Leave a trail in more detail.** It overlaps with the
   morning's cleanup: both organise a messy folder with a git save point. One
   option: refocus the exercise on reproducing Table 1 from the raw survey
   export, so the planted problem surfaces there.
3. **Course files.** `course-files.zip` (handout plus the three practice zips) is
   what people download from the course page, **vibing.jonasmoss.com** → Finance
   (on the menu deck's "Get the course files" slide). The page also has the
   handout and every deck. After any change to the handout or a prop: re-render, then
   `python3 make-course-files.py`, commit, push.
   Bring the zip on a USB stick too.
4. **Test on a BI-managed Windows laptop**, on campus wifi: install, log in, one
   prompt, one PDF read, and **git without admin rights** (the portable route).
   Also check that `/usage` (Claude Code) and `/status` (Codex) still show the plan
   limits in Friday's versions. Dagfinn's Codex install stalled in August until he
   picked the restricted (unelevated) mode. Codex reading PDFs on bare Windows is
   still untested.
   - **Tested 14 October on a BI PC:** the Claude Code install needed no admin
     rights, but asked for `.local\bin` to be added to PATH by hand. Fixed: the
     Claude install is now two lines, the second adds it to the user PATH.
   - **Not tested on a BI PC:** right-click → **Open in Terminal**, `explorer .`,
     and whether **Documents** sits in OneDrive. If it does, keep practice folders
     in the home folder (where `mkdir practice` puts them): git and OneDrive
     syncing don't mix well. Demo all three on your own Windows laptop live.
5. **Demo papers: to choose, a strategy paper this time.**
   - "Take a paper apart": your own pick, or one the room names on Friday morning.
   - Referee panel: Finance used Nagel (NBER w34104). For Strategy, one open paper
     you can download live. A candidate: Denrell and Liu (2012), "Top performers are
     not the most impressive when extreme performance indicates unreliability",
     *PNAS*, six pages and short enough to referee in the room.
   - Luck-test card: no paper needed (see "Your own work" below).
6. **The Foldnes example.** Make only the airtight claim: *the paper they cite does
   not exist; the DOI resolves to a 2022 editorial acknowledgement.* Don't say "the
   method doesn't exist" unless you've settled it with Foldnes. Details are in
   `scratch/examples/references/README.md`.
7. **Brief Ludvik.** In the morning he roams the install, Windows first. In the
   afternoon he's a second help desk. Tell him the rule: two minutes stuck, hand up.
8. **Room.** A2 Blue 1, booked 09:00–16:45. Check that power reaches every seat;
   bring extension cords.
9. **Pre-run the backups** on Claude: the Berger demo (one-line profile), plus one
   referee report from a fresh session.

**When behind:** cut talk, never hands-on time. The morning is tight and has no
buffer. If "Take a paper apart" runs over, let it run into the start of the
afternoon and drop one menu block. Don't cut the cleanup or the profile: they're
the spine.

**If the room can't decide on the afternoon,** take this default:

1. **References, with the claim check as the centre.** Everyone has a reference
   list, and catching one bad citation in your own field lands hard.
2. **Referee panel.** The most "I didn't know it could do that" of the four.
3. **Leave a trail**, if people are still keen, or straight into own work.

**Notes and structure** is the lightest module. It folds naturally into the end of
Leave a trail.

# Module cards

## Get it running

- **Aim:** a blinking cursor that answers, and `git --version` that answers, on
  every laptop.
- **Floor:** make a file, read it back, delete it.
- **Git is required now.** If someone has no admin rights, the agent installs the
  portable Git for Windows into their user folder. **Untested on a BI-managed
  laptop:** try it on Thursday. If it fails on the day, they pair with a neighbour
  for the git steps.
- **Watch for:**
  - the "x86" PowerShell;
  - skipping "close and reopen";
  - Command Prompt instead of PowerShell;
  - Codex's admin or sandbox prompt (choose unelevated);
  - git needing admin rights (the portable route, above).
- **People with no subscription** pair up. Don't let them sit idle.
- **Finished first?** They're the help desk. Say it out loud.

## Save points (git)

About 30–35 minutes, mandatory, straight after setup: 25 short slides and four
exercises (the yellow "Your turn" slides). New for Strategy: in Finance people
couldn't see how git differs from Dropbox or OneDrive.

- **The framing:** *mainly for the agent, very good for you too.* Four lines on
  what git is, then where it comes from (a timeline, two charts), so it reads as
  the tool the software world runs on, not a quirk of mine. Keep moving: most
  slides are one idea.
- **Talk, exercise, talk, exercise:**
  1. *A first save point* (3 min): git set up, a commit, "what changed?".
  2. *Undo* (2 min): revert, the history. "Done early?" is a branch.
  3. *A research project* (10 min): `props/founders-study.zip`, tidy, write a
     `.gitignore` with explanations, commit, then the privacy check.
  4. *Ask* (1 min): pick a word from the chips, ask what it means.
- **"What a save point is" is the slide people missed in Finance:** what a save
  point has to do with the files on their computer. Two clicks: commit (a full
  copy of every file goes into `.git`), then revert (a copy comes back out over
  the files). Say: *the files you see are always the current version. Delete
  `.git` and the history is gone, the files stay; copy the folder and the history
  comes along.*
- **The OneDrive slides are the ones to slow down on:** the per-file versions vs
  whole-folder snapshots diagram, then "40 restores vs one sentence". The line:
  *OneDrive is a backup, git is a lab notebook. Keep both.*
- **The theme for all jargon:** *unsure what a word means? Ask.* The chips slide is
  there to make the vocabulary look harmless, not to be learned. Worktree is the
  example because agents use it a lot (Claude Code has `--worktree`; parallel
  agents each get one).
- **The `.gitignore` exercise** (key: `scratch/examples/founders-study/README.md`).
  The folder has named transcripts, audio, consent forms, a survey with e-mails, a
  7 MB registry file, fake PDFs, a fake API key and junk files. Tested 20 October
  with Claude Code (one combined prompt, no approvals): 81 seconds; it moved
  everything sensitive into an ignored `local/` folder, explained each line, and
  on its own raised the two "v3 FINAL" drafts, the quotes in
  `coded_excerpts.csv`, and the pilots. Those three are the round-up.
  - **The bridge to the next deck:** ignored by git is *not* hidden from the agent.
    It read the transcripts to sort them.
  - **The download link** only works once Strategy is merged to `main` and pushed.
    The zip is also in `course-files.zip` under `practice/`.
- **"Revert to the last commit" was tested** on 20 October with Claude Code
  2.1.302 and Codex 0.162: both discarded the uncommitted change and nothing else.
  Claude also saved a backup patch first. *"Revert the last commit"* (no "to")
  would undo the commit itself; that's the small print on "You'll hear them back".
- **GitHub Pages:** free for public repositories on the free plan (GitHub's plans
  page, checked 20 October). The course page is one: say so, and say how little it
  took. Most teaching and personal pages are fine public. For private
  repositories, academics can get GitHub's academic plan (GitHub Education); the
  exact terms weren't checked (the docs pages had moved).
- **The name, if you want a laugh:** "git" is British slang for an unpleasant
  person. Torvalds: *"I'm an egotistical bastard, and I name all my projects after
  myself. First Linux, now git."* (as quoted in Scott Chacon's *Git Internals*,
  about 2008; the original occasion isn't pinned down).
- **Sources** (checked 20 October 2026):
  - Torvalds created git in April 2005 for Linux kernel development, after
    BitKeeper's free licence ended; first commit 7 April 2005; Junio Hamano has
    maintained it since July 2005. *Pro Git*, §1.2.
  - The survey chart: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2022, "Version control",
    professional developers (53,374 answering): Git 96.65%, SVN 5.96%, "I don't
    use one" 1.38%, Mercurial 1.22% (multiple answers allowed). All 71,379
    respondents: Git 93.87%. Don't say it's the latest survey that asked.
  - For a laugh, if it fits: in the 2018 survey, 7.9% of developers still listed
    "zip file back-ups" and 7.9% "copying and pasting files to network shares".
    That is how most of us still work.
  - Windows on git: 3.5 million files, about 300 GB, about 4,000 engineers;
    "the largest Git repo on the planet" is Microsoft's own title. Brian Harry,
    Microsoft DevBlogs, 24 May 2017.
  - The GitHub chart, milestones GitHub announced: over 40M developers (Octoverse,
    November 2019), 56M (December 2020), 100M (January 2023), over 180M
    (Octoverse 2025, 28 October 2025; 630M repositories). GitHub also said "over
    150 million" in August 2025; it's left out because it's a rounded milestone
    that makes a fake jump to October. Microsoft bought GitHub in 2018 for
    \$7.5 billion.
  - 2021 on the timeline is GitHub Copilot (technical preview, June 2021), which
    ran on OpenAI's Codex model, trained on public GitHub code (the Codex paper:
    54 million repositories; Chen et al. 2021). Not today's Codex agent.
  - Codex: *"requires commands to run inside a Git repository to prevent
    destructive changes"* (OpenAI, non-interactive mode docs; the override is
    `--skip-git-repo-check`). The error on the slide is real (Codex 0.162).
  - Claude Code checkpoints: *"Checkpointing does not track files modified by
    Bash commands."* (code.claude.com, Checkpointing).
  - Zenodo archives a GitHub *release* and gives it a DOI. The AEA Data Editor
    describes the route, but doesn't count GitHub alone as a trusted archive.
- **Handle with care:**
  - **Copilot and training:** GitHub says Copilot won't train on the repositories
    it indexes; what you send to Copilot on a personal plan can be used for
    training unless you opt out (since 24 April 2026).
  - **Git inside OneDrive** is advice, not established fact: no official
    Microsoft or git source was found that says it breaks.

## What it can touch

About 20–25 minutes, straight after git: 19 slides, three exercises. New for
Strategy: in Finance the room was far more worried about access than expected, and
got worked up when the agent opened the PDFs in the cleanup.

- **Why Finance got worked up:** since Claude Code 2.1.283 (September), *auto* is
  the starting mode for interactive sessions on every plan. Reading files in the
  folder needs no question, so the agent simply opened the PDFs. Say this out loud:
  it explains what they saw.
- **The stance, plainly:** lots of access, on purpose (my own `defaultMode` is
  `auto`). The 50th "yes" is never read; git makes mistakes cheap; auto mode stops
  what matters. Restrict the few things that matter, mostly by keeping them out of
  the folder.
- **Exercises:**
  1. *Where am I?* (2 min): see the mode, Shift+Tab, ask what it may do unasked.
  2. *A fence around the interviews* (5 min): a deny rule in `founders-study`,
     restart, try to read a transcript.
  3. *Check your switch* (1 min): the training setting on their own account.
- **What we tried** (20 October, a throwaway folder, `claude -p` with every
  prompt refused, so "asks" shows as blocked; Codex `exec` in `workspace-write`):
  - Claude, manual: reads in the folder and read-only commands (`ls`,
    `git status`) run; reading elsewhere (even via `cat`), writing, deleting and
    web pages all ask.
  - Claude, auto: edits, Python, reading outside the folder (interactive sessions
    ask once first, with four choices), a web page, `rm -rf data`, even
    `git reset --hard && git clean -fdx` went ahead. Posting a file to an outside
    address was stopped: *"denied by the Claude Code auto mode classifier.
    Reason: [Data Exfiltration]"*.
  - "Revert to the last commit" also works in auto mode (tested): the classifier
    weighs what you asked for. The docs list `git restore .` as blocked by
    default, so the explicit request is what makes it go.
  - Codex sandbox (Linux): reads anywhere, writes in the project and `/tmp`, a
    write to the home folder failed ("read-only file system"), network off.
  - The deny rule `Read(./interviews/**)`: blocked Claude's Read, `cat`, `cp` and
    a Python one-liner, but `grep -r Kari .` printed the transcript. Hence "a
    fence, not a wall".
- **Sources** (official docs, checked 20 October 2026):
  - Permission modes, starting mode, Shift+Tab order, auto mode's blocked and
    allowed lists: code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes. Auto works on all
    plans with recent models; Team and Enterprise admins can switch it off.
  - Settings files and rule syntax (`deny`, then `ask`, then `allow`):
    code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions and /settings. On Windows,
    `~/.claude` is `%USERPROFILE%\.claude`.
  - Claude's shell sandbox: off by default, and *"On native Windows, Claude Code
    runs commands unsandboxed"* (WSL2 needed). code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing.
  - Training: one consumer setting covers Claude Code; retention 5 years with
    training on, 30 days off. code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage.
  - Codex presets (Ask for approval, Approve for me, Full access), the
    auto-review reviewer agent, permission profiles that can deny reads, the
    Windows sandbox (elevated and unelevated; unelevated can't deny reads):
    learn.chatgpt.com/docs/sandboxing, /permissions, /windows/windows-sandbox.
  - ChatGPT: training controls apply to Codex; Business, Edu and Enterprise don't
    train by default. help.openai.com, "Using Codex with your ChatGPT plan".
- **Handle with care:**
  - **Labels on the settings pages** ("Help improve Claude", "Improve the model for
    everyone") weren't verified for October 2026. That's why the exercise sends
    people to the page instead of naming the switch. Check your own account
    before Thursday.
  - **"It sends what it reads"** is the honest short version, not a guarantee: a
    command's output can include many files, and connectors add other data flows.
  - **Personal data:** don't claim what BI's rules say unless you've checked.
    "Your consent forms and data plan decide" is safe.
- **If someone asks about `--dangerously-skip-permissions`:** it skips all checks;
  only for a throwaway machine. Not something to try on a work laptop.

## Do something tedious

About 25 minutes. The prop is `props/decrap-me.zip`, a synthetic WISEflow export:
15 group submissions with junk file names, cover sheets, and an empty grade sheet
in submission order.

- **Aim:** a reorganised folder, a grading table, and one deliberate undo.
- **The framing:** a job the chat window can't do, because it can't touch your
  files. Tedious, local, easy to judge.
- **Names only (new for Strategy).** Group and participant ID are in every folder
  name, so the job needs no reading. In Finance the agent opened the PDFs anyway
  (auto mode reads freely) and the room got worked up. Now the prompts say *"Work
  from the names only; don't open the submissions"*, and the last slide, "You decide
  what it reads", makes it the point. It follows straight on from the access deck.
- **The git beat:** they set up git an hour ago, so this is the habit, not the
  lesson. Brief the task, then ask *"Before you hit enter, does anything about this
  make you nervous?"* Answer with *"Set up git here and commit everything."*
- **The undo** is on purpose: delete the Marking guidance folder, then "revert to
  the last commit". Watching it come back is what makes git stick.
- **Done early?** Rename the fake papers in `founders-study/literature/` and make a
  `.bib`, without opening `interviews/`. The opposite case: there it has to read,
  and that's fine.
- **Ties forward:** "Leave a trail" and the GitHub demo reuse the same save-point move.

## What it knows about you

About 20 minutes. Two halves, framed honestly.

- **Opens with the field, as I imagine it (new for Strategy, 3–5 minutes).** Three
  cards: interviews and cases, regressions on firm data, "is it just luck?". Say
  plainly that you're a statistician guessing. Then *"Tell me what I got wrong"*:
  ask what's missing and who is which, and write their examples on the parking-lot
  board. Use those examples in the paper and referee blocks instead of yours. The
  last line, "the agent is in the same spot", is the bridge into the deck.
  - Sources for the cards: Burgelman's Intel fieldwork (*Strategy Is Destiny*, 2002;
    "Fading Memories", *ASQ* 1994); Eisenhardt (1989), "Building theories from case
    study research"; the diversification discount (Campa and Kedia 2002, Villalonga
    2004); luck and the CEO effect (Denrell and Liu 2012, Fitza 2014, Henderson,
    Raynor and Ahmed 2012). Background in `scratch/links/strategy-canon/`.
- **"Who you are" is an open question for this room.** In stats, in the terminal,
  you barely notice it; fields with schools may differ. Say exactly that, and let
  the room find out. Pairs pick opposite schools on *"Is strategy mostly planned,
  or does it emerge?"* (Ansoff and Porter vs Mintzberg and Burgelman). The round-up
  is data: *did it change, and how much?*
  - **Tested 21 October (Codex, three clean profiles):** all three answer "both".
    The profile changes the emphasis and the vocabulary, not the verdict: the
    planning profile defends deliberate direction and boundaries; the process
    profile explains it through Burgelman's induced and autonomous processes. So
    expect "it changed the framing", and ask the room whether that matters.
  - Another question that splits schools: *"How much does the CEO matter for firm
    performance?"* Tested the same day: every profile says "a lot, but no single
    number"; a Denrell-and-Fitza profile leads with luck, an upper-echelons profile
    with the bigger estimates.
- **The Berger demo** is the tested example of a school changing the answer. The
  A/B question with no profile, then one line in the folder's `AGENTS.md`:
  *"My intellectual idol is Jim Berger."* `/clear`, ask again. (Tested with
  `CLAUDE.md`; Claude reads `AGENTS.md` the same way as long as there's no
  `CLAUDE.md` in the folder or above it, so demo in a clean folder.)
  - Demo on **Claude**: Codex ignored the one-liner in testing.
  - The backup result is on the slide after the demo.
  - **If a statistician objects** that 0.91 is just 1 minus the one-sided p:
    they're right; under a flat prior it's the same information. The point is that
    the headline, the framing and the recommendation flip.
- **"How you work" is the reliable win.** The slide shows two lines from your own
  profile files (the 4-core rule, MathML). Your terminal profiles hold no "who I
  am" at all, only working rules, and you can say so.
- **The "who you are" profile belongs in the chat apps.** The homework slide says
  so, with your chat profile as the example. The coffee table ("Four askers") is in
  `more.html#/chat` if someone wants the chat-app version.

## Take a paper apart

- **Your demo:** a paper you can judge. Ask the three questions, and push at least
  once on camera.
- **Say these two sentences, no slide:**
  - when the first answers come back: *"It turned the PDF into text before it
    could read it"*;
  - when the fix runs: *"That script is the record of what it did."*
- **Snags:**
  - SSRN returns 403 to the agent: download in the browser, then "move it here".
  - The fix needs Python; let it install.
  - Codex on bare Windows may need a PDF tool; say yes.
- **Watch for:**
  - People skip *"Do they address it anywhere?"* and report false alarms. Collect
    one for the round-up.
  - Generic first answers are normal; *"what's specific to this paper?"* fixes most.
- **Honest framing:** *"I can't tell you whether a critique of a strategy paper is
  right. You can."* If it fails on someone's paper, say so in the round-up. That's
  a result too.
- **From the September pilots on two NBER finance papers:**
  - the critique took 1–1.5 minutes, the fix 5–7.5;
  - the two tools picked different "biggest problems" in the same paper.
- **Case studies and interview papers** work too, with different pushes (on the
  slide): *"Which claims rest on the fewest interviews?"*, *"What else would explain
  the same quotes?"* The "fix" is then a design (a comparison case, a sampling
  rule), not code.

## Referee panel

New module, not yet run with a room. About 40 minutes.

- **Aim:** two or three independent referee reports from one agreed procedure,
  plus an editor's letter.
- **Floor:** two reports from fresh sessions, and one concern they hadn't thought of.
- **The flow** (the diagram on the first slide):
  1. Who would referee this?
  2. **Ask how it's done:** a procedure, saved to `reviews/how-to-referee.md`.
  3. `/clear`, then one referee at a time, following the procedure.
  4. Not right? Change the procedure, not the report.
  5. The editor.
- **The lesson to sell beyond referees:** *ask the agent how a job should be done
  before you ask it to do it.* It's the most underused move. Step 2 is the place to
  say so out loud.
- **Why `/clear` and not a new window:** it's the same in both tools and needs no
  window juggling. After the procedure discussion, it's exactly right: each referee
  starts with only the paper and the procedure.
  - Parallel sessions are a one-liner for the eager: a second PowerShell window
    with its own `claude`/`codex`, or Claude Code's parallel subagents.
  - The agent can also start `claude -p` or `codex exec` in the background itself.
    Don't teach that today.
- **Skill hook:** "Turn the procedure into a skill called referee-panel" connects to
  the skills slide in `notes`, if anyone asks.
- **Demo:** the first two steps on a strategy paper, live. Then one referee from
  a fresh session.

## References

About 40 minutes for two of the four parts; 60 for all of them. Open with the
"in the literature right now" slide (3 minutes), then let the room pick parts.

- **Search.** Tell the story first: shallow, specific questions have turned up
  important papers you didn't know, in your own field (the Hjort–Glad prompt). Then
  the exercise, about 10 minutes: everyone asks one specific question about their
  own idea, and has it download the papers. The lesson is *be specific*. Deep ("I
  need every method since 1995…") is a different request: finalizing, slow, and
  expensive on usage. Show the prompt; don't run it in the room.
- **Papers in the folder.** The practice to sell hardest in this module: one rule in
  the project file (papers go in literature/; download what you can, a DOI for the
  rest), and the agent stops searching for the same paper again and again. It's
  also what makes the claim check work.
- **DOI check.** The practice `.bib` has six planted traps. The full key is in
  `scratch/examples/references/README.md`. Floor: three DOIs pasted into doi.org by
  hand.
- **Claim check.** The centrepiece. Run it on their *own* draft if they have one,
  after the papers are in literature/. "Not in the folder" is not "doesn't exist".
- **The line to end on:** *a polished bibliography is not evidence of a correct
  bibliography.*

## Leave a trail

About 50 minutes. The full instructor key is in `scratch/examples/leave-a-trail/README.md`.

- **One story: Reinhart and Rogoff.** Economists remember it, so ask the room first:
  *"Who remembers the 90% debt threshold?"* Keep it about their own interest, not
  open science: you want your rerun to find it before a grad student does. The
  facts, to stay accurate: above 90% debt to GDP they reported −0.1% average
  growth; Herndon, Ash and Pollin (2013 working paper; *Cambridge Journal of
  Economics* 2014) got +2.2%. The Excel range error (rows 30–44 instead of 30–49,
  dropping Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark) accounts for only about
  0.3 points of that; the rest is excluded years and the equal weighting by
  country. Don't say the Excel error alone flipped the result.
- **The folder is a practice project,** not their paper: Kari Nordmann's and their
  survey experiment on price framing (fictional), in `props/messy-project.zip`. The
  deck shows the link and the file tree. Those who finish go on to a copy of a real
  folder of their own, or the morning's paper folder.

- **Floor:** the rerun test passes after `/clear`.
- **Opening:** a show of hands, LaTeX or Word? LaTeX users already write in text;
  for them the news is git and the rerun test.
- **The practice folder** (`props/messy-project.zip`) has a planted problem. Three
  willingness-to-pay outliers were deleted by hand in Excel, with no record. With
  them in, the effect flips sign and stops being significant. Only the rerun test
  finds it.
- **The last-but-one slide is the reveal** ("What the rerun found": N = 223,
  −292 NOK, p = 0.26 with the three rows; N = 220, +53 NOK, p = 0.02 without). Show
  it only after the room has run the test. The handout only hints at it.
- **Git** was set up in the morning, so the exercise's first step is one prompt.
  Anyone who skipped the morning: the agent asks for a name and email at the first
  commit.
- **The test slide** is a diagram with two clicks: "Same numbers, done", then the
  loop back ("Not the same? Fix the README, run the test again").
- **Not yet piloted** with an agent end to end.

## Notes and structure

About 20–30 minutes; lighter than the rest.

- **The four questions** come from the `tidy-project` skill in this repo
  (`.claude/skills/tidy-project/SKILL.md`). It's a good live demo if someone asks
  "what does a real skill look like?"
- **"My paper folder"** is your `paper-init` layout (five folders: manuscript,
  code, results, dev, local), simplified: no justfile, Modal or Slurm. Say it's a
  skill, which sets up the skills slide at the end.
- **"dev/ or local/?"** is the one distinction worth slowing down for: `dev/` is
  committed (backed up on GitHub, co-authors see it) but never published;
  `local/` is in `.gitignore`, so git and GitHub never see it. It's also the
  natural place to say what `.gitignore` is.
- **Question 3** ("where are you allowed to be wrong?") is the one people stall
  on, and the stall is informative.
- **The log habit** (`notes/log.md`, then *"tell me where we left off"*) is the
  most useful thing in this module for people who'll use the tool weekly.

## Skills, if asked

Not taught. One slide at the end of the `notes` deck (`notes.html#/skills`) and a box in the handout.

- **The line:** memory is the AI remembering you; a skill is you writing it down.
- **When it's worth it:** a routine you repeat, want identical every time, or want
  to hand to a colleague.
- **Live demo if pushed:** open the `tidy-project` skill and show it's a page of
  plain English. Or, after any module: *"Turn what we just did into a skill called
  X"*, and show the file it wrote.

## The project file, if asked

- **The deck:** `agents.html`, about 10 minutes. The short version is already the
  last content slide of `notes`, and "Two files" in `knows`.
- **The practical answer people want:** one file, `AGENTS.md`. Codex always read
  it; Claude Code reads it since v2.1.277 (18 September 2026), but only when there's
  no `CLAUDE.md` in the folder or above it. An older repo with a one-line
  `CLAUDE.md` saying `@AGENTS.md` (like this course repo) still works.
- **Changes go through the agent:** *"Add to AGENTS.md: …"*. Nobody needs to open
  the file in an editor, though they can.
- **The habit worth selling:** *"Add that to the project file"* after the second
  identical correction.
- **`/init`:** fine as a shortcut, but the draft only describes the folder. The
  rules are the valuable part, and only they can write those. Claude Code's `/init`
  writes a `CLAUDE.md`, which would then hide the `AGENTS.md`: ask for `AGENTS.md`
  by name instead.
- **The gotcha:** both tools also read project files from the folders above.
  Starting the agent in Documents with a stray `AGENTS.md` there affects everything
  below it.

## GitHub, if asked

- **The deck:** `github.html`, about 10 minutes; section 12 of the handout.
- **The one-liner:** git is save points on your laptop, GitHub is the copy in the
  cloud. OneDrive syncs files; GitHub keeps every version and who made it.
- **Setup is one prompt** once they have an account: *"Install the GitHub
  command-line tool and log me in."* On Windows the agent runs
  `winget install --id GitHub.cli -e`, then `gh auth login`, which opens the
  browser. Not tested on a BI-managed laptop; if winget is blocked, the installer
  is at <https://cli.github.com>.
- **The selling point for research:** replication packages. A repository archived
  on Zenodo gets a DOI.
- **Say once:** private by default; history is forever, so data and passwords
  never go in.

### The pull-request demo, with Ludvik

About 10 minutes, live. It shows what collaboration *looks like* when neither of you
types a git command.

**Done live, from scratch.** No pre-made repository. If something breaks, narrate
the fix: watching the agent recover is part of the lesson.

**Before Friday:** Ludvik has a GitHub account, and `gh` installed and logged in.
Have his username ready.

**Setup, live (2–3 minutes):** in a copy of the "Leave a trail" practice folder
(`props/messy-project.zip`):
*"Set up git, commit everything, put this folder on GitHub as a private repository
called strategy-demo, and add [Ludvik's username] as a collaborator."* Ludvik
accepts the invitation (it comes by email), then: *"Download JonasMoss/strategy-demo
into this folder."*

**The pull request:**

1. **You, first:** start the watcher in Claude Code and let it sit:
   `/loop 1m check for new pull requests on this repository; when one appears, summarise it.`
   Test `/loop` beforehand. If it misbehaves, just ask *"any new pull requests?"*
   when Ludvik says he's done.
2. **Ludvik, on the projector or his own screen,** dictates or types:
   *"Make a new branch, add the missing rule to the cleaning (drop willingness to
   pay above 5,000 NOK; it was done by hand in Excel and never written down),
   rerun the analysis, commit, push, and open a pull request to Jonas explaining
   what you changed and why."* The practice folder has no cleaning script, so his
   agent writes one. That's fine, and it's a bigger change to review.
3. **You:** the watcher reports it. Then: *"Check out the pull request and test it.
   Rerun everything from the raw export: do we get table1 (N = 220)? And what
   happens without the new rule?"*
   - With the rule: N = 220, +53 NOK, p ≈ 0.02. The hand-cleaned file is now
     reproducible from raw.
   - Without it: N = 223, the effect flips sign (about −292 NOK) and stops being
     significant.

   That's why the rule has to be written down. Then: *"Comment: good catch, add
   the rule to the README too."*
4. **Ludvik:** *"Address Jonas's comment and push."* **You:** *"Merge it."*
5. **Show the pull request page in the browser:** the description, the comment,
   the commits, the merge. *"That page is the whole history of the decision."*

**Then the pairs exercise** (deck slide "Exercise: in pairs", handout section 12),
about 15 minutes: A puts a folder on GitHub and adds B; B accepts, downloads, and
opens a pull request; A reviews and merges; swap. Everyone needs a GitHub account
and `gh` logged in first, which is the slow part: start that during the demo.
Accepting the invitation through the agent goes through the GitHub API
(`gh api user/repository_invitations`); if the agent fumbles, the invitation email
has a button.

**Optional, if set up beforehand:** comment `@claude` (or `@codex review`) on the
pull request, and let the room watch a review appear on GitHub. This needs the
Claude GitHub app (`/install-github-app` in Claude Code) or Codex's GitHub
connection on the demo repository. Not yet tested.

## Your own work

- **Walk the room.** Ask "what are you trying?", not "is it working?"
- **Stuck people:** suggest *"What's here? What's missing? What would you do
  first?"* on a real folder, after a commit.
- **The luck-test card** is the one to push for this room: no data, a classic
  strategy question (Henderson, Raynor and Ahmed 2012, *"How long must a firm be
  great to rule out chance?"*), and a punchline people find themselves.
  - **Tested 21 October (Codex, 52 seconds):** 1,000 identical firms, a 50–50 year
    each, 30 years. **51 beat the benchmark in 20 of 30 years by pure luck**
    (49 expected); 8 had a 10-year winning streak; the longest was 14 years.
    Searching all firms and start years, an 18-year streak is the 5% bar, 20 years
    the 1% bar. Chosen *in advance*, 5 to 7 years would do. That last contrast is
    the point: picking the winners afterwards is what changes the arithmetic.
  - Good follow-ups: *"Now let skill differ a little. How often does the most
    skilled firm come out on top?"* (Denrell and Liu's question.)
- **Close:** *"What will you try on Monday?"* Get three answers out loud. Remind
  them the handout has everything, including what we skipped.

# Questions you'll get

The longer prepared answers are in `scratch/august-course/grievance-answers.md`.
The short versions:

- **"Is my data safe?"** What it reads is sent to the company, like any cloud
  upload. Keep out personal data and confidential material.
- **"Can it read my email?"** Yes, through connectors (MCP): Gmail, Google
  Calendar and Drive connect in a few clicks at `claude.ai/customize/connectors`,
  and Claude Code picks them up (`/mcp` lists them). Deck: `mcp.html`, five slides. BI
  mail is Outlook: a Microsoft 365 connector exists, but BI IT would likely have to
  approve it (not checked). Don't demo on your own work mail.
- **"Does it train on my data?"** It depends on the plan and changes over time, so
  check your plan's terms. When unsure, assume it could be retained.
- **"Claude or ChatGPT?"** Both are excellent. Use the one you pay for. They aren't
  interchangeable, so trying both on the same task is instructive.
- **"Will the department pay?"** That's a question for Dagfinn. Marketing
  reimburses its people via its administration.
- **"Can I get the slides?"** Yes: each deck is one file. Zip `decks/*.html` and
  send them to Dagfinn afterwards with the handout. Open `menu.html` first.
